title: Where are they now?

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: You walked up the ridge alone and gave the guardian what he came for. Those you sent away lived to tell it. Your name was carved on no wall, and that, the Keepers said, was the point.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: You gave yourself up to save the others, but they would not leave you. The guardian took the amulet home, and took you all with it. The barrier holds. No one knows who paid for it.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: The rite failed in the burial chamber. The guardian carried the amulet back to its cradle himself, over your body. The barrier holds, after a fashion. Akmentar keeps its secrets, and yours.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1928
variants.text: You came back with Eleanor Whitmore and never quite left her side. The story you told together was laughed at in London and believed in Cairo, which suited you both.

variants.caption: Marseille, 1929
variants.text: You and Isabelle Moreau went into business together, the kind with no fixed address. Some say you're still out there, a step ahead of someone.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1927
variants.text: You came back to Cairo and told the story exactly once, to a room that laughed. You never again showed much interest in ancient tombs, and you never sold the map.

variants.caption: London, 1932
variants.text: Her account of the forgotten king was published under her own name. Several of her conclusions remained controversial, but her work made her one of the leading authorities on the lost dynasty.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1934
variants.text: She published everything except the location. When pressed, she said some discoveries are best shared by keeping them, and that she had learned this from people she once called bandits.

variants.caption: Cairo Museum, 1929
variants.text: She kept her own notes and published nothing for years. When she finally did, she left out the parts no one would believe, and the expedition's leader along with them.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Eleanor Whitmore never came back from Akmentar. Her notebooks did. Someone at the museum still reads them.

variants.caption: Cairo Museum, 1926
variants.text: She stayed in the reading room, cataloguing other people's discoveries. She still keeps a rubbing of an erased cartouche in her desk drawer.

variants.caption: Oxford, 1930
variants.text: His meticulous record of Akmentar restored his reputation, if not his peace of mind. He catalogued everything except the last night, which he never described to anyone.

variants.caption: London, 1931
variants.text: His report was famous and furiously disputed. He defended every line of it, and quietly gave up fieldwork for good.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Arthur Pembroke died at Akmentar. His record survived him, every page numbered, and it was the most careful account anyone ever wrote of the place.

variants.caption: Cairo Museum, 1927
variants.text: He stayed at the museum, still waiting for the discovery that would put Wadi Natrun behind him.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1927
variants.text: He went back to the Keepers and told them everything, the attacks he ordered included. They let him stay. He spends his last years teaching them to keep watch without killing.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1929
variants.text: He returned to scholarship. His lectures on forgotten dynasties were packed, and he never once mentioned the organisation he had served.

variants.caption: Upper Egypt, 1928
variants.text: When the truth about the attacks came out, he left Cairo. Some say he lives in a village near the old wells, still watching the road west.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Hassan al-Masri died at Akmentar, trying to atone for the men he had sent against the expedition. The Keepers buried him as one of their own.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: He kept to Yacoub's back room and his books, and kept his secret. Nobody asked him again about Akmentar.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1929
variants.text: Tom founded a small security firm that took no contract involving leaving anyone behind. It did very well.

variants.caption: Haifa, 1928
variants.text: He went back to guarding crates for other men. He drinks less, and sleeps a little better.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Tom Hargreaves held the ridge, as he said he would. Nobody was left behind. He was the last one off it.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: He stayed at the club, telling the same stories to younger officers.

variants.caption: Omdurman, 1928
variants.text: He opened a shop in Omdurman with his share and never carried a gun again. His sisters both finished school.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1930
variants.text: Underpaid and over-risked, he went back to the trade he knew best, and became a man people in Cairo were careful not to cross.

variants.caption: Omdurman, 1927
variants.text: He went home, paid his family's debts, and stayed there.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Idris Mahjoub died at Akmentar. His earnings reached his sisters, as he had asked.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: He kept escorting merchants south, and never heard what happened at Akmentar.

variants.caption: Tangier, 1928
variants.text: She swore she was done with partners. She took one anyway, and the two of you were seen on three continents.

variants.caption: Marseille, 1929
variants.text: She founded her own security company. Its first rule: nobody tells anyone to stand down.

variants.caption: Somewhere, 1927
variants.text: She disappeared with her pay and her pistols, and was heard of only in rumours.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Isabelle Moreau died at Akmentar, fighting, in a position of her own choosing.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: She finished her business with the bounty men and left Cairo on the next boat.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1930
variants.text: Saleh retired with his reputation not only intact but doubled: the guide who brought people home from Akmentar.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1928
variants.text: He retired, and never again took travellers west of the last well.

variants.caption: The desert, 1926
variants.text: Saleh al-Rashidi died leading people to safety, which is how he would have chosen to go.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: He kept guiding caravans, and kept his record: everyone came home.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1931
variants.text: He became the famous explorer he had promised himself he would be: the man who found the road to Akmentar.

variants.caption: Faiyum, 1929
variants.text: He came back quieter. He became a fine caravan guide, and never once took a shortcut.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1928
variants.text: He became a respected caravan guide, and told the Akmentar story to every traveller who would listen.

variants.caption: The desert, 1926
variants.text: Youssef Nabil did not come home. He was not, in the end, afraid.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: He kept waiting at the caravanserai for the expedition that would make his name.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1930
variants.text: His trading posts along the expedition's road made him a rich man. He funded a chair in Egyptology, anonymously.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1929
variants.text: He retired wealthy and slightly ashamed of how much he had enjoyed doing something for nothing.

variants.caption: The coast road, 1926
variants.text: Farid Mansour died on the road. His accounts were found in perfect order.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: He kept moving goods between Cairo and twelve towns that are not on any map.

variants.caption: Luxor, 1929
variants.text: Mahmoud's crew was named in the record of every find. He founded an independent excavation team that the museums now ask for by name.

variants.caption: Luxor, 1927
variants.text: They went back to digging for other people's names.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Mahmoud Fawzi and several of his men did not come back. Their names are on no record of the finds.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: They were hired by the next expedition through Cairo, as they always were.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1929
variants.text: Khalil formed a workers' cooperative on the docks. Nobody in it has been cheated since.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1927
variants.text: They went home with their pay, which was more than some of them had expected.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Khalil Darwish died protecting his crew. They carried him home.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: They waited on the docks for work that came less and less often.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1930
variants.text: Naguib opened his own transport company. Its camels are never overloaded.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1928
variants.text: He became a sought-after expedition contractor, and always packs for the way out.

variants.caption: The road, 1926
variants.text: Naguib Sabet died on the road back. Everything was packed for the way out.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1926
variants.text: He went on building toward his own caravan, one contract at a time.

variants.caption: New York, 1927
variants.text: He sold the curse back to you for one thousand pounds and dined out on it for years. Nobody believed the second half of the story.

variants.caption: New York, 1927
variants.text: He lost the artifacts to you in a gunfight in Cairo and told the newspapers he had been robbed. He was not entirely wrong.

variants.caption: New York, 1928
variants.text: He gave the artifacts back under a black sky and never quite stopped telling people about it. His foundation now pays for excavations it is not allowed to profit from.

variants.caption: New York, 1927
variants.text: His expedition came home alive, thanks to you. He told everyone the wager was a draw, and paid it anyway.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: The American expedition never came home from its first night at Akmentar.

variants.caption: Berlin, 1929
variants.text: He accepted, at last, that some evidence must be returned rather than kept. His monograph on Akmentar contains no map.

variants.caption: Berlin, 1930
variants.text: He never forgave anyone for taking the artifacts back from him, and spent the rest of his career arguing that he had been robbed.

variants.caption: Berlin, 1928
variants.text: His expedition survived, and so did his reputation. His careful account of the surface ruins is still the standard work.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: The German expedition did not survive its first night at Akmentar.

variants.caption: Genoa, 1927
variants.text: The Italian expedition that stole the amulet was remembered, in Genoa, as unlucky. Bellini never went south again.

variants.caption: Genoa, 1927
variants.text: Bellini's trucks carried the survivors out of Akmentar. He took the credit, and for once deserved some of it.

variants.caption: Alexandria, 1929
variants.text: Danny flew the amulet home and dined out on it for years. His air service still flies the desert route, though never at night.

variants.caption: Alexandria, 1928
variants.text: Danny delayed a gang of thieves with a misfiled booking and never charged for it. He still says you owe him a drink.

variants.caption: Alexandria, 1926
variants.text: A pilot in Alexandria, who might have been a friend, kept flying mail and questionable cargo.

variants.caption: Cairo Museum, 1928
variants.text: He signed Hassan al-Masri's export ban, and afterwards insisted on hearing everything. He rewrote the museum's records himself.

variants.caption: Cairo Museum, 1930
variants.text: Faced with the re-carved Wall of Hieroglyphs, he revised the museum's records himself, though he never admitted in public that he had been wrong.

variants.caption: Cairo, 1938
variants.text: He went to his grave insisting that Akmentar was a camel drivers' story, and that whatever you found there was something else.

variants.caption: London, 1927
variants.text: He paid for the expedition's survivors to go home in comfort, published Ashby's report, and accepted what it said about him.

variants.caption: London, 1927
variants.text: He never forgave you for refusing him the amulet, and never sponsored another expedition.

variants.caption: London, 1935
variants.text: He kept his first expedition's secret to the end. It was found among his papers.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1927
variants.text: The Keepers lost most of their number at Akmentar, and their mission succeeded. Those who remain keep watch with fewer rifles and more patience.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1927
variants.text: The Keepers were all but destroyed. The few who remain still watch the road west.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1930
variants.text: Noura led the Keepers after her uncle, and ended their war on travellers. She believes keeping a secret should not require killing for it.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Noura died before the rite was finished. Omar sang her part.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Noura al-Khatib kept the ceremonies, as her family always had, far from any foreigner's eyes.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1931
variants.text: Omar succeeded Rashad as the Keepers' commander. He keeps a foreigner's rifle on his wall, and tells young guardians where it came from.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1930
variants.text: Omar dedicated his life to guarding Akmentar.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Omar fell before the rite was finished, defending the woman who taught him.

variants.caption: Akmentar, 1926
variants.text: Omar Saqr went on riding with the Keepers, hating foreigners a little less than before, or a little more.

variants.caption: Alexandria, 1928
variants.text: Freddie paid back every penny he owed you, eventually, and most of what he owed everyone else.

variants.caption: Alexandria, 1927
variants.text: Finch caught up with Freddie in Alexandria. He is still paying, from a cell.

variants.caption: Somewhere, 1927
variants.text: Freddie vanished again. Postcards arrive from time to time, never with a return address.
